shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner on a visual approach in the evening, arriving at the airport where the pilot flying was based. There was weather to the west of the airfield, and the winds at altitude were gusty tailwinds.

The crew. The report comes from the pilot flying, who had experience of approaches to this airport as a pilot based there. It does not say whether the pilot flying was the captain or the first officer, and gives no flying hours.

What happened. The crew flew a published visual approach procedure. Because of the weather west of the field and the gusty tailwinds at altitude, the aircraft was slightly high on the final segment. To get back to the landing aim point, the pilot flying pushed the nose down further than the pilot flying normally did on approaches to this airport. Passing 500 ft above the ground the aircraft was descending at 1,800 ft per minute, which was outside the company's normal standard operating procedures, and the ground proximity warning system gave three "Sink rate" alerts. The pilot flying corrected the rate of descent before 300 ft. The crew continued the approach and landed.
safe_outcome: The aircraft landed without further incident. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: The aircraft could not be stopped on the remaining runway. It left the end of the runway at about 30 knots and came to rest on the grass. The passengers were evacuated, and two received minor injuries during the evacuation. The aircraft was slightly damaged.
notes: Rule 3 removed: the whole "Cause" section ("compression", "get-there-itis", "last leg syndrome", "in the future I will go around", "improper application of delayed descent"). "Last leg" was not used as a fact because it appears only inside that label. Rule 5 moved to the safe ending: the uneventful landing (from the synopsis). Judgement calls: "a 3 alert GPWS sink rate call out" is read as three "Sink rate" alerts; the report does not say whether the reporter (the pilot flying) was the captain or the first officer, and the crew paragraph says so; no light or weather conditions are coded, so "in the evening" is from the 1801-2400 time block and the approach is described as visual, as the report does; the SOP exceedance is the reporter's own statement and is given as a fact. A short report: the shared text is within range with nothing added.
